source_text: Ἐπεὶ δ᾿ ἐπὶ πλέον κεκωμῴδηκε τὴν κεκηρυγμένην μὲν τῆς σαρκὸς ἀνάστασιν ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ὑπὸ δὲ τῶν συνετωτέρων τρανότερον νενοημένην. καὶ οὐ χρὴ αὖθις ἐκτίθεσθαι τὴν λέξιν αὐτοῦ ἅπαξ προειρημένην· φέρε καὶ περὶ τοῦ προβλήματος τούτου. ὡς ἐν τῇ πρὸς ἀλλότριον τῆς πίστεως ἀπολογίᾳ γραφομένῃ διὰ τοὺς ἔτι νηπίους καὶ κλυδωνιζομένους καὶ περιφερομένους „παντὶ ἀνέμῳ διδασκαλίας ἐν τῇ κυβείᾳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, (ἐν πανουργίᾳ) πρὸς τὴν μεθοδίαν τῆς πλάνης.“ ὀλίγα ἐστοχασμένως τῶν ἐντευξομένων κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμῖν ἐκθώμεθα καὶ παραστήσωμεν. οὔτε μὲν οὖν ἡμεῖς οὔτε τὰ θεῖα γράμματα αὐταῖς φησι σαρξὶ, μηδεμίαν μεταβολὴν ἀνειληφυίαις τὴν ἐπὶ τὸ βέλτιον, ζήσεσθαι τοὺς πάλαι ἀποθανόντας, ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἀναδύντας· ὁ δὲ Κέλσος ἡμᾶς συκοφαντεῖ ταῦτα λέγων. ἀκούομεν γὰρ καὶ πολλῶν γραφῶν περὶ ἀναστάσεως ἀξίως θεοῦ λεγουσῶν, ἀρκεῖ δ᾿ ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος τὴν Παύλου παραθέσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς πρὸς Κορινθίους προτέρας λέξιν, φάσκοντος· „ἀλλ᾿ ἐρεῖ τις· πῶς ἐγείρονται οἱ νεκροί; ποίῳ δὲ σώματι ἔρχονται; ἄφρον. σὺ ὃ σπείρεις οὐ ζωοποιεῖται, ἐὰν μὴ ἀποθάνῃ· καὶ ὃ σπερίρεις, οὐ τὸ σῶμα τὸ γενησόμενον σπείρεις ἀλλὰ γυμνὸν κόκκον, εἰ τύχοι, σίτου ἤ τινος τῶν λοιπῶν· ὁ δὲ θεὸς δίδωσιν αὐτῷ σῶμα, καθὼς ἠθέλησε, καὶ ἑκάστῳ τῶν σπερμάτων ἴδιον σῶμα.“ ὅρα γὰρ τίνα τρόπον ἐν τούτοις „οὐ τὸ γενησόμενον σῶμά“ φησι σπείρεσθαι, ἀλλ᾿ ἀπὸ τοῦ σπειρομένου καὶ γυμνοῦ βαλλομένου ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν λέγει διδόντος τοῦ θεοῦ „ἑκάστῳ τῶν σπερμάτων ἴδιον σῶμα“ οἱονεὶ ἀνάστασιν γίνεσθαι, ἀπὸ τοῦ καταβεβλημένου σπέρματος ἐγειρομένου στάχυος ἐν τοῖς τοιοῖσδε, οἱονεὶ ἐν νάπυϊ ἢ ἐπὶ μείζονος δένδρου ἐν ἐλαίας πυρῆνι ἤ τινι τῶν ἀκροδρύων.
thought_title: The seed and the body that is to be
pass_a_gloss: But since he has mocked (κωμῳδέω, pf.) at greater length the resurrection (ἀνάστασις) of the flesh (σάρξ), proclaimed (κηρύσσω) in the churches (ἐκκλησίαι) but understood (νοέω) more clearly (τρανότερον) by the more intelligent (συνετώτεροι) — and there is no need (χρή, neg.) to set out (ἐκτίθημι) again his wording (λέξις) once already stated — come (φέρε), also about this problem (πρόβλημα), as in a defence (ἀπολογία) written to one alien (ἀλλότριος) to the faith (πίστις), on account of those still infants (νήπιοι) and tossed by waves (κλυδωνίζομαι) and carried about (περιφέρω) 'by every wind of teaching (διδασκαλία), in the dice-play (κυβεία) of men, in craftiness (πανουργία), toward the scheming (μεθοδεία) of error (πλάνη)', let us set out and present (παρίστημι) a few things, aiming (στοχάζομαι, adv.) at those who will read (ἐντυγχάνω, fut. ptc.), as far as is possible for us. Neither we nor the divine writings (θεῖα γράμματα) say that with the very flesh (αὐταῖς σαρξί), having taken up no change (μεταβολή) for the better, those who died long ago will live (ζάω), having come up (ἀναδύω) from the earth; Celsus slanders (συκοφαντέω) us saying this. For we hear many scriptures (γραφαί) speaking about resurrection worthily (ἀξίως) of God, but for the present it suffices (ἀρκέω) to quote Paul's wording from the first to the Corinthians, saying: 'But someone will say, How are the dead raised? With what sort of body do they come? Senseless one (ἄφρων). What you sow (σπείρω) is not made alive (ζωοποιέω) unless it dies; and what you sow, not the body that will be (γενησόμενον) do you sow, but a bare (γυμνός) grain (κόκκος), it may be (εἰ τύχοι) of wheat or of one of the rest; but God gives it a body as he willed (θέλω), and to each of the seeds (σπέρματα) its own (ἴδιος) body.' For see in what manner in these he says 'not the body that will be' is sown, but he says that from what is sown and thrown bare onto the earth, God giving 'to each of the seeds its own body', as it were (οἱονεί) a resurrection comes about, an ear (στάχυς) being raised from the seed cast down, in such things, as it were in mustard (νᾶπυ), or in the case of a greater tree in the stone (πυρήν) of an olive or of one of the tree-fruits (ἀκρόδρυα).

only 'rising up from the earth' kept as Celsus's words; 'in the very same flesh' unquoted (Origen drops ἐκείναις)

pass_b_english: He has mocked at some length the resurrection of the flesh, which is preached in the churches but understood more clearly by the wiser. There is no need to set out his words again, since they have already been quoted once. Come, then, let us set out and present a few things on this problem too, as far as we can, with an eye to those who will read this, as befits a defence addressed to one who is a stranger to the faith and written for the sake of those who are still infants, tossed by waves and carried about “by every wind of doctrine, by the trickery of men, in craftiness, toward the scheming of error” (Ephesians 4:14).

Neither we nor the divine writings say that those who died long ago will live, “rising up from the earth” in the very same flesh, flesh that has received no change for the better; Celsus slanders us in saying so. For we hear many scriptures speaking of the resurrection in a way worthy of God, but for the present it is enough to quote Paul’s words from the First Letter to the Corinthians, where he says: “But someone will say, ‘How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?’ Foolish one! What you sow is not made alive unless it dies. And what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind; but God gives it a body as he willed, and to each of the seeds its own body” (1 Corinthians 15:35–38).

See how in these words he says that it is “not the body that is to be” that is sown, but that from what is sown and cast bare upon the earth, as God gives “to each of the seeds its own body,” a kind of resurrection takes place, as a stalk rises from the seed cast down in plants such as mustard, or, in the case of a larger tree, from the stone of an olive or of some fruit tree.
notes: The quoted phrase “rising up from the earth” repeats Celsus's wording at 5.14 (ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἀναδύντας) in the English used there; αὐταῖς σαρξί (Origen drops Celsus's ἐκείναις) is left unquoted as 'in the very same flesh'. στάχυς rendered 'stalk' here and at 5.22, since Origen applies it to mustard as well as grain. The opening Greek sentence (Ἐπεὶ ... φέρε ... ἐκθώμεθα) is split into three English sentences; the staged text's full stops after νενοημένην and μεθοδίαν τῆς πλάνης are editorial and break one period. Ephesians 4:14: Origen's text adds ἐν πανουργίᾳ in parentheses as in Koetschau; κυβεία ('dice-play') rendered 'trickery'. Staged text has the typo σπερίρεις for σπείρεις; read σπείρεις. In 1 Corinthians 15:37 τῶν λοιπῶν rendered 'some other kind'. The mustard example may echo the parable of the mustard seed (Matthew 13:31–32), but Origen does not quote it; left uncited. ἀκρόδρυα = fruit trees with hard-shelled fruit (nuts and the like); rendered 'fruit tree'. 'in plants of this sort' renders ἐν τοῖς τοιοῖσδε (that is, grain such as wheat).
